newsitem.title: USA: Universal studios perfecting "scream park" concept.
newsitem.headline: Universal studios perfecting "scream park" concept.

text.p: Though the roaches were pampered with a diet of peanut butter and pure water so they wouldn't get sick while performing, but the music, vibration and lights negatively affected their psyches.
So officials at Universal Studios Florida in planning their sixth "Halloween Horror Nights" did away with the "Roach Wranglers" show.

It was all part of the planning for the celebration of Halloween at central Florida's myriad theme parks -- a celebration that has helped turn October from one of the area's slowest months of the year for tourism to one of the busiest.

Many of Orlando's parks and attractions, from Disney World to Gatorland, are hell-bent on spooking their customers for Halloween on Oct. 31, when Americans traditionally celebrate a night of ghosts, ghouls and costumes.
Still, not all has gone smoothly in the past.

For example, Universal scratched its "Spider Man" and "Snake Woman" shows because the tarantulas hired to play themselves ended up escaping to the theme park's synthetic spider webs and snakes slithered down Hollywood Boulevard after their performance.

But Universal kept the ever-popular "Rat Lady" -- who sits in a box with live rats crawling over her body -- and added an unprecedented 400 other horrifying characters in an ever more elaborate scare-fest cooked up to combat tourism doldrums in October, traditionally Orlando's slowest month.

The effort that began in 1991 as a weekend event called "Fright Nights" has evolved into a multi-million dollar extravaganza which rattles on for 15 nights over three weeks from mid-October past Halloween.
The Halloween gimmicks include three high-tech spookhouses -- one called "Toy Hell," a pawn shop transformed into a nightmarish attic with evil toys that come to life at night.

In addition, more than 1,500 severed and decaying "limbs" are strewn throughout Universal's park, a parade of ghouls floats down the street and a marching brigade of bloody chainsaw "killers" terrorises guests.

Universal officials will not discuss profits or attendence figures, but say the event -- which requires more than 600 gallons of fake blood, brain fluid and sludge -- has boosted attendence by about 70 percent.

"October is one of our busiest times of the year thanks to Halloween Horror Nights, but if you look at the statistics, October has been one of the slowest months of the year in central Florida," said Fred Lounsberry, Universal's vice president of marketing.
Street parties in downtown Orlando feature actors in costume mingling with pedestrians. The Shakespeare Festival and Southern Ballet Theatre launched productions of "Dracula".

Disney World transformed its Magic Kingdom into a friendly Halloween party called "Mickey's Not-So-Scary-Halloween." It differs dramatically from Universal's spread, which issues a disclaimer warning parental discretion for children younger than 13.
Sea World of Florida continues its traditional Halloween Family Sleepover which invites children in grades K-3 and their parents to spend the night in the marine park.

Universal offered a special "Ghoulish Getaway" vacation package created for state residents but now especially popular with international travelers, particularly Japanese tourists, said park spokesman Wit Tuttell.
The event provides holiday income for hundreds of locals. Packs of people from all walks of life auditioned for roles as scary characters.

"The way I look at it, on the one hand you have a bunch of really bizarre characters that jump out at you from dimly lit cubicles at work and here at Universal they've got haunted houses so there isn't much difference," said Ken Stricker, 37, an engineer who plays an undertaker in this year's "Festival of the Dead" parade.

Stricker says it beats the office where co-workers carry slide rules and pin Dilbert comics to cubicle walls. "I saw this in the paper three years ago and came out and auditioned and ended up as a screaming portrait in the psycho house. Last year I worked as a psychotic chainsaw killer and this year I'm an undertaker. I kind of look at it as therapy."
The most coveted roles are the devil, which requires a fit male actor, and the rat lady, who has become an icon of sorts.

"I cannot believe the number of people who will travel hundreds of miles to play the rat lady," said Jerry Abercrombie, Universal's manager for creative entertainment. The park hired six actresses to work with the rats in shifts.
